record.paper_title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems
record.original_question: How can rule-changing games be given concrete game-theoretic models and solution concepts when domain-theoretic approaches to games closed under rule change face unresolved obstructions, including powerdomain constructions that do not fully capture desired standard game-theoretic features?

evidence.quote:
This is a remarkable tour de force , which uses much of the machinery in domain theory developed
up to that point in building these intricate models of economic behaviour, in which self-reference and
self-modification are central. However, the limiting features of domain theory itself seem to have led to
unresolved obstructions to further progress. In particular, the non-set-theoretic nature of powerdomains
means that, in lifting standard solution concepts from game theory to the domain theoretic setting, the
desired features are not fully captured.
Once again, as in the case of the biological modelling, a gap remains between the mathematical theory
and the concrete models one wishes to capture.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A "rule-changing game" is an extensive form of strategic interaction in which the rules of the game (the set of admissible moves, payoff functions, and even the set of players) may themselves be modified by the moves of the players, so that the space of possible games is closed under such rule changes and admits self-reference (a game whose rules can refer to and alter the game itself).

One known approach to modeling such self-referential games is via domain theory: one seeks a domain D (a directed-complete partial order with a suitable bottom element) such that D is isomorphic to a space built from D using powerdomain constructions (e.g., the Plotkin, Smyth, or Hoare powerdomain) together with function-space and product constructors, so that elements of D represent games whose moves can lead to other elements of D. However, powerdomains do not in general yield set-theoretic powerset-like objects, and standard game-theoretic solution concepts (such as Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium, correlated equilibrium, or evolutionarily stable strategies) lifted to this domain-theoretic setting fail to fully capture their classical features.

Problem. Provide a mathematically rigorous framework for rule-changing games that:
(i) gives a precise definition of a rule-changing game as a mathematical object closed under rule modification and admitting self-reference;
(ii) defines analogues of standard solution concepts (at minimum a Nash-type equilibrium and a subgame-perfect-type refinement) within this framework;
(iii) proves existence theorems for these solution concepts under reasonable hypotheses; and
(iv) either resolves the obstructions arising from the non-set-theoretic character of powerdomain constructions when lifting these solution concepts, or replaces the powerdomain approach with an alternative construction that faithfully reproduces the desired classical game-theoretic features.
artifact.status_search_result: No widely cited resolution of the problem of providing fully satisfactory game-theoretic models and solution concepts for self-referential, rule-changing games appears in the literature. Domain-theoretic models of such games (e.g., work by Vela Velupillai and collaborators on computable economics, and Edalat-style domain-theoretic constructions) are recognized as partial but incomplete, and standard search does not reveal a definitive resolution.
